description: Six curated color pairs specifically optimized for moiré work. Organized by intended interference effect.

pairs.name: Red-Cyan Maximum Vibration
pairs.description: True complementary pair in OKLCh, matched lightness, maximum chroma. The definitive moiré vibration pair.
pairs.usage_notes: Use at 1:1 area ratio and equal stroke weight. The eye will be unable to average the colors — every grid intersection produces chromatic flicker. At high spatial frequencies (small grid), this becomes dizzying. Reduce chroma of one color to 0.5 to dial down the intensity.

pairs.name: Violet-Lime Maximum Vibration
pairs.description: Blue-yellow opponent axis at maximum chroma. Activates both opponent channels simultaneously.
pairs.usage_notes: Note the asymmetric lightness in OKLCh — violet is perceptually darker than lime at the same HSL L. To match perceived luminance, raise lime's L to ~0.45 or lower violet's to ~0.55. Maximum vibration occurs when OKLCh L values match, not HSL L values.

pairs.name: Blue-Orange Harmonic Resonance
pairs.description: Complementary pair with reduced chroma — readable interference pattern without harsh vibration. Classic landscape palette applied to moiré.
pairs.usage_notes: Enough contrast to produce a clear moiré pattern but not enough to vibrate uncomfortably. The orange reads warm, the blue reads cool — the interference fringes create a warm-cool oscillation. Works at both fine and coarse grid scales. Increase saturation of both to push toward vibration territory.

pairs.name: Teal-Rose Harmonic Resonance
pairs.description: Split-complementary-adjacent pair. The colors don't directly oppose — they share an axis of tension that produces interference without discomfort.
pairs.usage_notes: Controlled interference — the moiré reads as a subtle shimmer rather than chromatic vibration. The reduced saturation keeps both colors in the 'sophisticated' register. Works well for architectural visualization and long-duration viewing. The rose reads warm, the teal cool; fringes oscillate between the two temperatures.

pairs.name: Navy-Cream Subtle Interference
pairs.description: Low-saturation analogous-range pair. The moiré pattern reads as luminance variation rather than chromatic contrast — subtle texture, no vibration.
pairs.usage_notes: The dominant effect here is value contrast (light vs. dark), not hue contrast. The moiré produces a gray-scale luminance pattern — classical, print-like, appropriate for technical contexts. The slight warm-cool undertone gives the interference a barely perceptible chromatic quality. Use when you want the moiré pattern to be felt as texture rather than color.

pairs.name: Muted Triadic Subtle Interference
pairs.description: Two colors from a muted triadic set. The 120° hue distance creates mild hue contrast without complementary tension. The moiré pattern reads as a soft colored texture.
pairs.usage_notes: Very quiet interference. The moiré reads almost as a neutral gray-green shimmer. The 120° hue angle is far enough for the colors to read as distinct but close enough that the eye can partially average them at overlap points. Excellent for backgrounds that need depth without drama. Matching OKLCh lightness is what keeps this from vibrating despite the hue gap.
